product_description: Solid Khaya (African mahogany) electric guitar in headless and headed series, carrying a reduced embedded electronics package. A performance instrument: amplified through the dry output jack, with wireless monitoring and onboard effects.

construction.body_architecture_note: Solid Khaya blank with routed cavities. Cavity placement is materially harder than in the hollow sibling: each pocket needs wall thickness to its neighbours, which is what forces the reduced electronics package.

series.note: Shares the headless bridge and locking nut with the Smart Guitar.

Flying V profile headstock with 6-inline locking tuners for straight string pull. Adds roughly 190 mm of overall length and replaces the headless bridge tuners with conventional ones. Body, neck, and cavities are otherwise identical to the headless series.

components: Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB) — JACK + Guitarix/MODEP host and coaching engine
Teensy 4.1 — I/O coprocessor, control only, no audio path
Battery pack + BMS (2x 18650), USB-C PD charging
40 mm cooling fan, lid-mounted, venting outward
MOTU M2 USB audio interface — EXTERNAL, not mounted in the instrument
electronics_package.rationale: Full Pi 5 compute is retained onboard; audio moves entirely to an EXTERNAL MOTU M2. The M2 replaces two components at once — the Hi-Z USB input interface and the HiFiBerry HAT — because it provides instrument input, line output and headphone output in one productised unit. That matters beyond convenience: a HiFiBerry is an excellent converter board but solves none of the guitar-specific analog problems. Using it would still require designing a Hi-Z input stage, instrument preamp, gain control, headphone amplifier, protection circuitry and analog filtering. A USB interface has already solved all six. Dropping the HAT and its GPIO ribbon channel frees 148 cm2, taking this line from 25 cm2 short to roughly 123 cm2 spare, so the packing stops being borderline. An external box is appropriate here because this is a performance instrument played at an amplifier or a pedalboard.
electronics_package.external_components_note: MOTU M2 measures 190.5 x 108 x 45 mm and weighs 0.61 kg. It CANNOT be mounted internally: 45 mm of height in a 47 mm blank leaves 2 mm for both skins even at zero floor, and its footprint with margins is 283 cm2 against 287 cm2 of usable body area — 99%, which would displace every other component. The M2 remains EXTERNAL and is therefore compatible with the sourcing policy: it is a peripheral the customer connects, not a component designed into the instrument. Were it mounted internally the policy would forbid it regardless of fit.
electronics_package.open_question: Whether this line eventually carries the custom onboard front end developed for the Smart Guitar, replacing the external M2 and unifying the two electronics architectures. The onboard audio front end is therefore a CUSTOM SUBASSEMBLY, not a sourced product. It is bounded engineering rather than open-ended: a USB audio codec plus a JFET Hi-Z input stage, both of which have vendor reference designs. It still has to solve the six things a converter board does not — Hi-Z input impedance, instrument preamp, gain control, headphone amplifier, protection and anti-alias filtering. COST CLASS IS DIFFERENT FROM A SOURCED PART: it carries non-recurring engineering for schematic, layout and prototyping, plus EMC certification for the finished assembly, against a per-unit BOM well below any retail interface price. The budget model must carry NRE and certification as separate lines rather than folding them into unit cost. Physical envelope is not the constraint: the 36 mm height limit was derived against retail enclosures, and a bare board is a fraction of that.

provenance.note: Split from a single conflated product record on 2026-07-27. This line carries BOTH headstock series; the Smart Guitar line is headless only.

notes: STATUS IS 'concept'. Like its sibling, this instrument exists as an AI-generated image and a set of derived dimensions, not as a measured object.

Packing is comfortable in this configuration, roughly 123 cm2 spare, because audio is external. It was NOT comfortable before: carrying the HiFiBerry HAT onboard left the line 25 cm2 short with a 2x 18650 pack and within about 1 cm2 only if part margins tightened from 4 mm to 3 mm. That borderline case is the reason the HAT was dropped, not an argument that it could have stayed.

Configurations that do NOT fit a solid body of these dimensions, retained so they are not re-derived: full stack including the HiFiBerry HAT, 96 cm2 short; same with a 4x 18650 pack, 25 cm2 short. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W with a HiFiBerry Zero fits (+31 cm2) but costs roughly five times the compute. The MOTU M2 cannot be internal in any configuration: 45 mm tall in a 47 mm blank.
The headed series is concept_defined and gated behind the headless first article, so its extra hardware is a documented delta rather than a costed variant.
onboard_audio_output false is the single functional difference from the Smart Guitar and is a use-case decision, not a compromise: a stage instrument does not need a headphone jack.
Contains no cost, price, or margin fields by design.

Bus-powering the M2 from the instrument battery costs runtime: about 4.7 h on a 4x 18650 pack versus 6.3 h for the Pi alone, and about 2.3 h on the 2x 18650 pack specified here. If runtime matters, power the M2 from the host rather than the instrument.

SOURCING POLICY — NO EMBEDDED THIRD-PARTY CONSUMER PRODUCTS. A finished retail product may not be designed into either instrument as an internal component. Embedding one creates OEM licensing and trademark exposure, a single-source dependency on another company's product roadmap, warranty and support ambiguity, and re-certification questions for the finished assembly. This rules out mounting an iRig HD 2, Apogee Jam X, Scarlett Solo or MOTU M2 inside the body, regardless of whether it physically fits. EXTERNAL peripherals are NOT affected: shipping or recommending an interface the customer connects is resale, not embedding.
